# Mahābodhijātaka (Ja 528)

**ID:** Ja 528
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahābodhijātaka* (Ja 528) is a major narrative preserved in the Pannāsanipāta of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1891]. According to its opening frame, the Buddha related the narrative at Jetavana concerning the Perfection of Wisdom (*paññāpāramī*), illustrating how in a previous existence he had crushed all philosophical disputants [Fausböll 1891]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born into a wealthy family as Bodhikumāra and later renounces the world to become the wandering ascetic Mahābodhi [Fausböll 1891; Anandajoti 2010]. After taking up residence in the royal park at the king's invitation, palace intrigue and false suspicion lead the king to plot against his life, prompting Mahābodhi to depart while giving verses on true friendship, treachery, and the impropriety of overstaying one's welcome [Anandajoti 2010].

The philosophical core of the text centers on Mahābodhi's rebuttal of five heterodox doctrines maintained by five corrupt royal counselors [Jayatilleke 1963; Omvedt 2003]. These five viewpoints represent non-causality (*ahetuvāda* / denial of kamma), creation by a supreme lord (*issaranimmāna*), past-action determinism (*pubbekatavāda*), annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and political statecraft (*khattiyavijjā* or Kshatriya doctrine), the last advocating that one must pursue self-interest even through violence or parricide [Omvedt 2003; Jayatilleke 1963; Sinha 1991; Narada 2008]. When accused by the ministers of wrongdoing after appearing with a monkey skin, the Bodhisatta applies a *modus tollendo tollens* refutation, demonstrating that under any of their respective philosophical premises, killing cannot be condemned as an evil deed [Jayatilleke 1963; Elverskog 1997]. In the commentary's identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the five errant ministers are identified as the five classic heretical leaders (Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Pakudha Kaccāna, Ajita Kesakambalī, and Nigaṇṭha Nāthaputta), and Mahābodhi is identified as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1891; Pande 1974].

 DharmaNexus automatically matches portions of the text with the Tibetan *Jātakamālā* (D4150), the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra*, and the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada* [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Pali canon, this jātaka forms the subject of story 23 in Āryaśūra's Sanskrit *Jātakamālā*, is depicted in early Buddhist narrative art at Bhārhut, and is preserved in bilingual Sanskrit-Uighur manuscript fragments discovered at Sängim [Martin 2006; Elverskog 1997].
